content.content:
# Writing the benchmark spec

perfproof measures one command, the benchmark, and checks one test
command. You write both into a JSON spec and lock it with
`perfproof bench define <name> --spec <file> --json`. Locking records the
hashes of the files listed in `harness`, `oracle`, `inputs` and
`config`, so a later change that edits them is refused.

Keep the spec file in `.perfproof/specs/<name>.json`. Show the user the
command, the test command and what is compared, in one short paragraph,
before you lock it.

## Choosing the benchmark

- It runs the code the user cares about, the way it is really used, on
  realistic input. Not a microbenchmark of one line.
- One run is long enough to be far above the timer's step, and short
  enough that dozens of runs fit in the time the user will wait. Tell
  the user the expected total before you start.
- It is deterministic: fixed seeds, fixed input files, no network.
- If the code under test has its own timing, have the benchmark print
  one line `PERFPROOF {"value": <seconds>}` on stdout and use the
  `reported` metric. That times only the work, not interpreter start-up.
  Otherwise use `wall`.

## Where the benchmark lives

The baseline is a fresh checkout of the commit, so a file you wrote and
did not commit is not in it. Put a benchmark you wrote under
`.perfproof/harness/` (for example `.perfproof/harness/bench_x.py`) and
list it in `harness`. perfproof copies that directory, byte for byte,
into both versions before anything runs, and a change cannot touch it.
Once one file there is listed, every file in the directory is locked,
so put helper modules beside the benchmark and expect an edit to any of
them after locking to be refused. Only `.git` and `__pycache__` are
ignored: any other file that appears or changes there after the freeze
(a cache the benchmark writes beside itself, a `.DS_Store`) fails the
lock gate, so tell the benchmark to write caches outside that directory.
That includes a candidate directory the user hands you: its own
`.perfproof/harness/` is replaced, so keep nothing of theirs there.
Run it from the repository root with `cwd` `"."`.

Do not point the command at `.venv/bin/python` or another ignored path
without `setup`: the baseline checkout has no such directory. Add
`"setup": {"commands": [["uv", "sync", "--frozen"]], "timeout_seconds":
600}`, which builds each version's own environment, and run the
benchmark with `uv run --frozen python ...` (plain `uv run` may
re-resolve) or `.venv/bin/python ...`, which then
exists in both. Never use the main checkout's environment: an editable
install there would import its source in both versions.

## Choosing the checks

- `correctness.command`: the project's tests for that code, or the whole
  suite if it is fast. A failing test on the new code rejects the change.
- `correctness.outputs`: files the benchmark writes that must be the
  same in both versions. Use `numbers` for numeric output (with a
  tolerance only if the user says results may differ slightly), `text`
  or `bytes` otherwise. Make the benchmark write its result to a file
  if it doesn't.
- `correctness.coverage_command` (optional, with
  `correctness.coverage_timeout_seconds`): only for a change in a
  language other than Python, and only when the project has a coverage
  tool. A command that runs the tests under it and writes lcov or
  Cobertura to the path in `$PERFPROOF_COVERAGE_REPORT`. Python needs
  none. Leave it out when unsure: changes in other languages are then
  measured but not kept, with "no coverage command declared".

## Template

```json
{
  "schema_version": 4,
  "name": "<name>",
  "command": ["python", "bench.py", "--output", "out/result.npy"],
  "cwd": ".",
  "env": {},
  "metric": {"kind": "reported", "direction": "lower_is_better", "unit": "s"},
  "objective": "wall_time",
  "guardrails": [
    {"metric": "peak_memory", "direction": "lower_is_better", "unit": "bytes",
     "allowance": 0.1, "allowance_source": "default"},
    {"metric": "peak_gpu_memory", "direction": "lower_is_better", "unit": "bytes",
     "applicable": false, "reason": "no GPU is used"},
    {"metric": "p99_latency", "direction": "lower_is_better", "unit": "s",
     "applicable": false, "reason": "serves no requests"}
  ],
  "correctness": {
    "command": ["python", "-m", "pytest", "-q", "tests/test_thing.py"],
    "cwd": ".",
    "timeout_seconds": 300,
    "outputs": [{"path": "out/result.npy", "compare": "numbers"}]
  },
  "warmup": 1,
  "budget": {"max_rounds": 60, "max_seconds": 1800},
  "looks": {"n0": 10, "k": 10, "max_looks": 6},
  "min_effect": 0.03,
  "alpha": 0.05,
  "timeout_seconds": 120,
  "harness": ["bench.py"],
  "oracle": ["tests/test_thing.py"],
  "inputs": [],
  "config": [],
  "allow_runtime_change": false,
  "allow_cross_host": false
}
```

## Fields worth knowing

- `command`: run a Python script, or a program built in the
  repository. A shell in between (`sh -c`, a `.sh` script) or an
  installed program outside the repository can't be identified, and
  the runtime check refuses it.
- `metric.kind`: `wall` (whole command), `cpu`, `reported` (the
  `PERFPROOF` line), `counter` (Linux only). `wall` and `cpu` are in
  seconds and lower is better.
- `guardrails`: list all three as above. Mark one `applicable: false`
  with a short true reason when it does not apply.
- `setup`: `{"commands": [[...], ...], "cwd": ".", "timeout_seconds": N}`.

content.content:
- `setup`: `{"commands": [[...], ...], "cwd": ".", "timeout_seconds": N}`.
  Argv commands run once in each version before the first run, outside
  the timing, with the same environment as the benchmark. It must not
  need credentials or a remote service.
- `reset`: if the benchmark changes something outside its own process
  (a local database, a cache directory), add
  `"reset": {"command": [...], "timeout_seconds": 60}` to put it back
  before every run.
- `budget` and `looks`: use the template's values (60 rounds, `n0` 10,
  `k` 10, `max_looks` 6), the provisional defaults the decision rule is
  calibrated under. Depth changes how many ideas you try, not these.
  `n0` and `k` must be even.
- `min_effect`: the bar. A change is kept only if even the low end of
  its range beats `1 + min_effect` (3% by default). Change it only if
  the user states a different bar.
- `harness`, `oracle`, `inputs`, `config`: the benchmark files, test
  files, input data and config files to lock. Paths relative to the
  repository. Those under `.perfproof/harness/` are installed in both
  versions by perfproof. Never lock the code you are trying to speed
  up, or any file the change you are proving touches: a change to a
  locked file is refused, so the change could never be measured. A
  benchmark the change adds or edits goes into `.perfproof/harness/` as
  a copy instead (see SKILL.md, prove step 3).

If `bench define` refuses the spec, its JSON `error.message` says why.
Fix that field; don't loosen a check to get past it.
# Rust

Read this when the code to speed up is Rust, built with cargo. The
method is the same as everywhere else; what differs is how to launch
the benchmark so the toolchain can be identified, what first runs cost
(there is no JIT), how to profile compiled code, and where Rust code
usually loses time.

## Launch the benchmark so the toolchain can be identified

`compare` only keeps a change when it knows what runs each version. It
reads a built binary: the compiler that made it is in the file. It does
not follow `cargo run`, `cargo bench`, `rustc` or `rustup`: rustup
chooses the toolchain (a `rust-toolchain.toml` can change it), and
`cargo run` builds before it starts the program, which would put the
build inside the timed run. Those give `runtime` `not_available` and a
KEEP is withheld. Build in `setup`, which is not timed and not checked,
and run the binary itself:

```json
"setup": {"commands": [["cargo", "build", "--release", "--locked"]],
          "timeout_seconds": 1800},
"command": ["target/release/<name>", "<arguments>"]
```

- Always `--release`, and `--locked` so the dependencies are the ones
  in `Cargo.lock`. A `target/debug` binary is unoptimised code, and
  rarely what the user runs: say so if the user's own command is one.
- Give both versions the same build: the same `cargo` command, features
  and `RUSTFLAGS`. A change to the `[profile]` in `Cargo.toml`
  (`lto`, `codegen-units`, `opt-level`, `panic`) is part of the change
  under test, and perfproof does not compare it between the two trees;
  read it in the diff, and say that a change of it is a change of the
  build and not of the code.
- A library crate has no binary. Write a small harness crate under
  `.perfproof/harness/bench/` with the crate as a path dependency and an
  empty `[workspace]` table (so cargo does not take it for a member of
  the project's workspace), run `cargo generate-lockfile --manifest-path
  .perfproof/harness/bench/Cargo.toml` once before locking (a lockfile
  written later would change the locked directory), and build it in
  `setup` into a directory of its own:

  ```
  ["cargo", "build", "--release", "--manifest-path",
   ".perfproof/harness/bench/Cargo.toml", "--target-dir",
   "target/perfproof-bench"]
  ```

  The command is then `target/perfproof-bench/release/bench`. Pass the
  inputs and results through `std::hint::black_box`, or the compiler
  may fold a constant loop away.
- Native code and the project's own tests are run the usual way: the
  `correctness` command may be `cargo test --release --locked`.

## Warm-up

Compiled Rust has no JIT, so there is no in-process warm-up to wait
for and no stop rule to write. Two small effects remain; the numbers
are in "Warm-up (Rust)" of `docs/method.md`, from one busy machine:

- The first execution of a freshly built binary was several times
  slower than later ones in one macOS series. Set the spec's `warmup`
  to at least 1, as a precaution.
- The first iterations inside one process were slower than most later
  ones in one busy-machine series, which did not separate a warm-up from
  noise. If the benchmark loops in process and prints one number
  (`reported`), discard its first few iterations (5 is a guess) and
  loop a fixed number of times. Never loop until the time settles: a
  loop that can fail to settle must not fail the execution.

A command line tool is measured whole (`wall`); a library function is
looped in process.

## Profile

`perfproof profile` runs any command that writes folded stacks. The
system profilers write their own formats, and Rust symbols arrive
mangled, so `perfproof.profilers.rust` runs the binary under `sample`
(built into macOS) or `perf` (Linux) and writes folded stacks with
demangled symbols:

content.content:
demangled symbols:

```
perfproof profile <name> --json --own-module <binary name>
  --profiler-command '["<python>", "-m", "perfproof.profilers.rust",
  "record", "--output", "{output}", "--project-root", "<repo root>",
  "--", "{command}"]'
```

`<python>` is the Python that perfproof itself runs in: the `python`
beside the `perfproof` executable. `--own-module` is the binary's file
name: the profile then marks the crates that the repository defines
(the `Cargo.toml` files under the root name them) as project code, and
the standard library, the dependencies and C code linked in as library
code.

What to know when reading the result:

- A frame is ``<binary>`<crate>::<module>::<function>``. There is no
  file or line: a Rust path says where to look (`my_crate::parse::tokens`
  is in the crate `my_crate`, module `parse`, so `src/parse.rs`, or
  `src/parse/mod.rs`, or an inline `mod parse`). `grep` for the
  function.
- The command must be the built binary. A command that starts the
  binary through `cargo run` or a shell is profiled as cargo or the
  shell.
- On macOS `sample` records every thread, running or parked, from a few
  tens of milliseconds after the start; the wrapper drops threads parked
  in a blocking call and says how many samples that was on stderr. The
  share is of the samples kept. A run of well under a second gives few
  samples: run the workload longer. On Linux the CPU-clock event counts
  only running threads, and a stack needs frame pointers: build the
  profiled binary with `RUSTFLAGS="-C force-frame-pointers=yes"` into
  its own `--target-dir` (the timed binary stays as it was), or add
  `"--call-graph", "dwarf"` to the command (not run here; it needs debug
  information in the binary). In a container, libc frames
  can show as `[unknown]`, and frames in the kernel as `[kernel]`.
- The compiler inlines. A small function called in a loop has no frame
  of its own: its time is in the caller, and a hot caller whose body is
  one loop is the answer. The same holds for the standard library
  (`Vec::push`, `contains`), where the growth or the comparison shows
  only if it was not inlined.
- Neither profile shows time a thread spends waiting (macOS: the
  wrapper drops parked threads; Linux: the event counts running time
  only): if CPU time is well below wall time, look at locks and I/O,
  not at the loops.

## What usually goes wrong, and the cheap test for each

Run the test on the profile's top frames before writing a change. Each
is a count or a share, never a timing to report.

| Suspect | What the profile shows | Cheap test |
|---|---|---|
| Growing a `Vec` or `String` that has a known length | allocator frames (`realloc`, `_szone_realloc`) high; `RawVec` growth frames (`finish_grow`, `do_reserve_and_handle`) where not inlined | count allocations per call with the allocator below; `with_capacity(n)` or `reserve(n)` leaves one |
| Cloning, `to_vec`, `to_owned`, `collect` into a temporary | allocator frames (`malloc`, `free`, `__rdl_alloc`) at the top, and `<String as Clone>::clone`; the cloning function's own share small | the allocation count per call against the number of items: one per item means a copy per item; borrow (`&[T]`, `&str`, `Cow`) instead |
| Formatting in a loop (`format!`, `to_string`, `println!` to build text) | `core::fmt::` frames plus allocator frames | allocations per call; `write!` into one reused `String` allocates nothing per item |
| Iterator chains | nothing named: adapters inline into the caller. Suspects are a `collect` in the middle, `.chars().count()` or `.nth()` re-walking a string, `Vec::contains` or `iter().position` inside a loop, `remove(0)` and `insert(0, ..)` | run the same code at `n` and `2n` and compare how the sample count in the caller grows (twice is linear, four times is quadratic); count comparisons rather than timing |
| Bounds checks | the whole loop in one function, no frame to blame | disassemble the function (`llvm-objdump -d --disassemble-symbols=<symbol> <file>`, from `rustup component add llvm-tools-preview`, find the symbol with `llvm-nm`): a compare and branch to `core::panicking::panic_bounds_check` inside the loop is the check. Only tight numeric loops are worth it: iterate over the slice, use `zip` or `chunks`, or check the size once before the loop |
| Hashing with the default `HashMap` | `hashbrown` frames with high self share (SipHash is inlined into them); `SipHasher` frames where it is not | a copy of the loop with a trivial `BuildHasher` or a `Vec` indexed by the key bounds what hashing costs; a hasher from a crate is a new dependency, so ask first |
| Locks and shared counters | `Mutex::lock_contended`, `__psynch_mutexdrop`, futex frames; CPU time below wall time | the same work on one thread against `N` threads: one thread being as fast means the lock serialises it; batch updates per thread, shard, or use atomics |

content.text:
I tried one change, buffering fd's output, and the correctness checks passed. perfproof can't give a verdict yet, so I haven't kept or rejected it. The change is committed on `perfproof/fd-light`. You're back on `main` with a clean working tree.

**Goal:** the wall time of `fd -H -I . eval-tree`, which lists about 20,000 paths. The bar was that the low end of the range must be above 3%.

**Profile.** I profiled a longer version of the same listing, because the original run was too short to sample. About 39% of the samples were reading directories, inside the `ignore` crate rather than fd's own code. Another 29% were under `fd::output::print_entry`, almost all of it `write` calls.

**Idea tried.** Rust's stdout is line-buffered, so every printed path cost its own `write` call. I put a 64 KB buffer in front of stdout. It is flushed whenever the result channel runs empty, so streaming output isn't held back. It is also flushed at the end. The change touches `src/output.rs` and `src/walk.rs`. From the profile, this part of the run can save at most about 1.4x. That is a bound, not a result.

**What was checked and passed:**
- `cargo test --release` passed.
- Locked benchmark files were untouched, the runtime was identified, and the machine was the same.
- No side effects were found.
- I also checked by hand that the sorted output of the listing is the same, though I didn't compare it against the original.

**The timing:** perfproof can't keep changes yet. The estimate is 1.46 (range 1.42 to 1.52), not yet a verdict.

**Not checked:**
- Coverage: perfproof can't see which Rust lines ran, because no coverage command is declared. A keep would also need that check.
- Peak memory: it isn't measured yet. The new 64 KB buffer is the only change that touches memory.
- Machine load: the machine was busy (load around 6.5 to 7.5 on 10 cores). This only widens the range.
- Behaviour: I didn't test Ctrl-C or `| head`. Output still buffered when you press Ctrl-C may be lost.

The full record is at `.perfproof/runs/20261023T103918Z-246f56/report.md`.

**What is left:** directory reading (39% of the profile) is inside the `ignore` crate. I didn't try it, because changing it means changing a dependency.

Shall I leave the attempt on `perfproof/fd-light` for you to judge, or delete the branch?

Result: INCONCLUSIVE (insufficient_evidence)
